subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 8 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Consecutive-square pattern and the meaning of an algebraic identity

textbook_items_in_class.description: Demonstrates that for three consecutive square numbers, adding the smallest and largest and subtracting twice the middle square always gives 2, checked with two numeric sets.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to choose any three consecutive integers and compute their squares. Have them add the smallest and largest squares, then subtract twice the middle square, and record the result. Repeat with a second set. Ask: what do you notice? Collect results on the board without confirming the pattern yet.

Work through Example 1, p.68 together, naming the three numbers n-1, n, n+1 in symbols. Show the algebraic steps that confirm the result is always 2. Discuss why this is surprising and what makes it an identity rather than an equation with specific solutions.

Think-and-reflect: ask students in pairs to test whether four consecutive squares have a similar invariant when you take alternating signs (i.e. largest minus second minus third plus smallest). Students conjecture first, then check numerically with two sets of four consecutive integers, and share findings.

Whole-class discussion: distinguish between a numerical result that happens to hold and an algebraic identity. Introduce the language: an identity holds for all values of the variable. Students write a one-sentence summary of today's key idea in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter by letting students encounter an algebraic identity through a numerical surprise before any formal definition is given. A common error here is students believing the invariant might be a coincidence specific to the numbers they chose — push them to try odd, even, and large integers to build conviction before the algebra confirms it. For a student ready to go further, Example 1, p.68 can be re-read with n replaced by a fraction.

periods.activity_title: Visualising and applying the binomial-square identity (a+b)²
periods.visual_aids: Partitioned square of side (a+b) drawn on the board: one square of side a, one square of side b, two rectangles of area ab

textbook_items_in_class.description: Verifies (a+b)^2 = a^2+2ab+b^2 for negative values a=-2, b=-3.
Expands (5x+2y)^2 using the identity.
Computes 43^2 as (40+3)^2 using the identity.
Expand six binomial-square expressions.
Find (64)^2, (105)^2, (205)^2 using the identity.

time_bands.activity: Draw a square of side (a+b) on the board and partition it into four regions: an a×a square, a b×b square, and two a×b rectangles. Label each region's area. Sum the areas to read off (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b². Then derive the same result algebraically using the distributive property, so students see both routes give identical results.

Work through Example 2, p.70 (negative values), Example 3, p.71 (binomial with coefficients), and Example 4, p.71 (computing 43²). After each example, pause and ask students to identify which letter plays the role of a and which plays b.

Think-and-reflect: ask students to compare (a+b)² and a²+b² for a=3, b=4, then for a=0, b=5. When is (a+b)² larger than a²+b²? When are they equal? Students write their reasoning and discuss in pairs before sharing. Then ask: if you replace b by −b in (a+b)², what identity do you expect to get?
Quick individual practice: Exercise 4.1 Q1 (i)–(iii) and Q2 (first two values). Students solve independently while the teacher circulates and checks for sign errors in the 2ab term.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that algebraic identities hold universally, this unit develops the first and most-used identity through both geometric and algebraic derivations. The most frequent error at this stage is writing (a+b)² = a²+b², omitting the 2ab term entirely — the geometric picture showing two rectangles of area ab is the strongest corrective. Students who finish early can attempt Exercise 4.1 Q1 (iv)–(vi), which include fractional and reciprocal-form terms.
homework: Complete Exercise 4.1 Q1 (iv)–(vi) and Q2 (third value, 205²) from p.71–72.

periods.activity_title: Factorisation using perfect-square identities and introducing (a−b)²
periods.visual_aids: Geometric diagram for (a−b)² derived by removing an (a−b)×b strip and a b×b square from an a×a square

textbook_items_in_class.description: Factors x²+4x+4 as (x+2)².
Factors 36x²+12x+1 as (6x+1)².
Factors 50p²+60pq+18q² by extracting common factor 2, then matching to (5p+3q)².
Computes 29² as (30−1)² using (a−b)².
Factor four quadratic expressions using the perfect-square identity.
Find (79)², (193)², (299)² using (a−b)².

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: if expansion means going from (x+2)² to x²+4x+4, what is the reverse process? Take x²+4x+4 and ask students to identify what a and b would have to be. Work through Example 5, p.72 and Example 6, p.72 as guided class examples, naming the matching step explicitly each time.

Work through Example 7, p.72: students often miss the common factor. Demonstrate that checking for a common factor before matching is a reliable first step. Ask: if you did not pull out the 2 first, would the identity still match? Let a student try to confirm it does not match directly.

Derive (a−b)² = a²−2ab+b² on the board: start from (a+(−b))² and apply the (a+b)² identity with b replaced by −b. Draw the geometric split of an a×a square. Work through Example 8, p.73 to show the computational application. Connect back to the consecutive-squares pattern from section 4.1 and show the algebraic proof using (n−1), n, and (n+1).

Students work on Exercise 4.2 Q1 (i)–(iv) and Q2 (first two values) individually, then compare answers with a partner. Circulate and prompt students who are unsure whether to use the plus or minus form of the identity.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the expansion of (a+b)², this unit reverses the direction — matching a given quadratic to the identity pattern — and introduces (a−b)² as a natural consequence of substituting −b. A persistent error is writing the middle term of (a−b)² as +2ab instead of −2ab; asking students to substitute a specific value to check their factored form is an effective self-correction habit. Example 8, p.73 can serve as a self-study model for students who want to practise numerical applications independently.

periods.activity_title: Deriving and applying the three-term square identity (a+b+c)²
periods.visual_aids: Partitioned square of side (a+b+c) showing nine regions: three squares and six rectangles

textbook_items_in_class.description: Computes 119² as (100+10+9)² using the three-term square identity.
Find six squares using suitable identities.
Factor five expressions using suitable identities.
Expand (p+3q+7r)² and (3x−2y+4z)² using the three-term square identity.
Determine whether (a+b−c)²+(a−b+c)²+(a−b−c)² = 2a²+2b²+2c² is an identity.

time_bands.activity: Derive (a+b+c)² on the board: substitute d = b+c into (a+d)² = a²+2ad+d², then expand d² = (b+c)² and 2ad = 2a(b+c). Collect all terms to arrive at a²+b²+c²+2ab+2bc+2ca. Draw the nine-region partitioned square and ask students to label each region's area — confirming the algebraic result geometrically. Think-and-reflect: can students identify which squares and rectangles correspond to which terms?

Work through Example 9, p.76 together: decompose 119 = 100+10+9 and apply the identity. Ask students to suggest an alternative decomposition (e.g. 119 = 120−1) and compare the effort required by each approach.

Students work in pairs on Exercise 4.3 Q3 (expand (p+3q+7r)² and (3x−2y+4z)²) and Q1 (two or three values of their choice). The (3x−2y+4z)² example requires treating −2y as the second term; circulate and watch for sign errors in cross-product terms.

Whole-class: take Exercise 4.3 Q4 — is (a+b−c)²+(a−b+c)²+(a−b−c)² = 2a²+2b²+2c² an identity? Students expand the left side and simplify. Discuss how to verify an identity claim versus disprove it with a counterexample.

periods.teacher_notes: Having derived the two-term square identities, this unit extends the technique to three terms by a substitution step that reuses the earlier identity. The most common error when expanding (a+b+c)² is missing one or more of the three cross-product pairs (2ab, 2bc, or 2ca), so listing all nine regions of the diagram before collecting terms helps students keep track. For further practice, Exercise 4.3 Q2 and Q5 can be assigned as self-study using the same matching strategy.
homework: Complete Exercise 4.3 Q1 (remaining values not done in class) and Q2 (i)–(iii) from p.76–77.

periods.activity_title: Algebra tiles: representing factorisation as rectangle construction
materials: Paper cut-outs or drawn tile grids (x² tile, x-tiles, unit tiles)
periods.visual_aids: Tile rectangle diagram on the board: (x+3)(x+4) as an x²-tile, seven x-tiles, twelve unit tiles arranged into a rectangle

time_bands.activity: Introduce the three tile types: an x²-square tile, an x-by-1 rectangular tile, and a 1×1 unit tile. Ask students to represent x²+7x+12 by placing one x²-tile, seven x-tiles, and twelve unit tiles on their desk or on the board. Challenge them to arrange all tiles into a single rectangle without gaps or overlaps.

Guide the class to discover that 7x must be split as 3x+4x to form the rectangle: one dimension is x+3 and the other is x+4. Show why splitting as 2x+5x or 1x+6x fails to produce a valid rectangle. The think-and-reflect question is woven here: let a volunteer try a different split and show the class whether a valid rectangle results.

Extend to (2x+3)(3x+1): ask students how many x²-tiles, x-tiles, and unit tiles appear in the product. Work out the count together (6x², 11x, 3), sketch the rectangle, and identify the two binomial side lengths from the arrangement. Students then attempt (x+5)(x+2) independently with their tiles or a tile sketch.

Think-and-reflect debrief: use algebra tiles to find factors of x²+5x+6 — students set up the rectangle and identify both side lengths. Discuss how the tile model connects to the factorisation (x+2)(x+3) and what the rectangle dimensions tell us about the factors.

periods.teacher_notes: The tile model in this section makes the abstract middle-term-splitting step concrete and spatial; students who work through it physically or with sketches are much better prepared for the symbolic method that follows. A common point of confusion is believing any split of the middle term should work — the rectangle constraint is what rules out invalid splits, and this insight is worth dwelling on. Students who want more practice can use the think-and-reflect prompts from section 4.5 to try other expressions with algebra tiles.

periods.activity_title: Splitting the middle term symbolically and factorising quadratics

textbook_items_in_class.description: Factors x²+7x+12 by finding a,b with a+b=7 and ab=12, giving (x+3)(x+4).
Factors x²+11x+30 giving (x+5)(x+6).
Factors x²−5x+6 with negative a and b.
Fill in the blanks to complete four factorisation identities.
Compute eight products/squares using suitable identities.
Factor five algebraic expressions using identities.

time_bands.activity: Recall the tile model: to factor x²+bx+c we need two numbers a and b whose sum is the coefficient of x and whose product is the constant term. Formalise: x²+(a+b)x+ab = (x+a)(x+b). Work through Example 10, p.81 — list factor pairs of 12, identify the pair summing to 7, and write the factored form.

Work through Example 11, p.81 and Example 12, p.81. In Example 12, both numbers are negative — ask students why. The think-and-reflect thread: pose the debate from section 4.6 — if a student claims (a−b)²(a+b) can be derived two different ways, ask the class to work out both and judge which is correct. This reinforces careful handling of signs.

Students work individually on Exercise 4.4 Q1 (fill-in-the-blanks) and Q3 (i)–(iii). Then pairs swap papers and check each other's sum-and-product reasoning. Circulate to catch errors where students find numbers with the right sum but wrong product or vice versa.

Whole-class: take one expression from Exercise 4.4 Q2 (e.g. 23×17 written as (20+3)(20−3)) and demonstrate that identifying a near-square is a smart application of identity choice. Students complete Q2 (remaining values) and Q3 (iv)–(v) as a quick-finish task.

periods.teacher_notes: Having seen the tile model's physical reasoning, students now formalise it into the sum-and-product search. The most frequent error is choosing a and b with the correct product but the wrong sign on their sum — reinforce checking both conditions simultaneously. Example 11, p.81 provides a clean second worked model that students can re-read as self-study if they need another demonstration before attempting the exercises.
homework: Complete Exercise 4.4 Q2 (any remaining values) and Q3 (v) from p.81–82.

periods.activity_title: Binomial cube identities, sum and difference of cubes, and the three-variable cube identity
periods.visual_aids: Geometric decomposition of a cube of edge (a+b) into two cubes and six cuboids — sketched on the board

textbook_items_in_class.description: Finds the cube root of p³+6p²q+12pq²+8q³ by matching to (a+b)³.
Finds the cube root of 8n³−60n²m+150nm²−125m³ by matching to (a−b)³.
Uses the three-variable cube identity to find the sum of cubes given sum, product, and sum of squares.

time_bands.activity: Derive (a+b)³ by writing it as (a+b)(a+b)² and expanding step by step using the distributive property and the known identity for (a+b)². Arrive at a³+3a²b+3ab²+b³. Sketch the cube decomposition on the board (two cubes, six cuboids) and identify which term each piece contributes. Substitute −b for b to write down (a−b)³ = a³−3a²b+3ab²−b³ and ask students to verify the signs.

Work through Example 13, p.84 and Example 14, p.84: matching a polynomial to the (a+b)³ or (a−b)³ template requires identifying a and b from the first and last terms. Ask: how do you check whether the middle terms also match once a and b are chosen? Think-and-reflect: as the power rises from x²−y² to x³−y³, does (x−y) remain a factor? Students reason briefly in pairs before the teacher confirms with direct expansion.

Derive x³−y³ = (x−y)(x²+xy+y²) and x³+y³ = (x+y)(x²−xy+y²) by direct polynomial division or by expanding the right-hand side. Then state and expand x³+y³+z³−3xyz = (x+y+z)(x²+y²+z²−xy−xz−yz), and work through Example 15, p.85 to show how the identity converts a sum-of-cubes problem into a product of known quantities.
Quick consolidation: pose two short problems — (i) expand (2m+3n)³ and (ii) factor a³−27b³ — for students to solve individually. Review on the board, checking sign patterns carefully.

periods.teacher_notes: The derivation of (a+b)³ is a direct application of the earlier binomial-square identity; highlighting this connection helps students see the chapter as a developing toolkit rather than isolated formulas. A common error when applying (a−b)³ is getting the signs of the 3a²b and 3ab² terms wrong — the geometric cube diagram, which shows all six cuboids as positive volumes, clarifies why both middle terms carry their own sign determined solely by the power of b. Example 13, p.84 makes a good self-study model for students who want to practise the template-matching step independently.

periods.activity_title: Simplifying rational expressions and applying factorisation to geometric problems

textbook_items_in_class.description: Simplifies (x²−7x+12)/(5x²+5x−100) by factoring and cancelling the common factor (x−4).
Finds length and breadth of a rectangle by factoring x²+8x+15.
Finds the dimensions of a rectangular pool of area 96 sq. m by factoring x²−4x−96=0.
Simplify six rational expressions by factoring and cancelling common non-zero factors.

time_bands.activity: Introduce rational algebraic expressions by analogy with numerical fractions: just as 12/8 simplifies by cancelling the common factor 4, an algebraic fraction simplifies by factoring numerator and denominator and cancelling common polynomial factors (provided the cancelled factor is non-zero). Work through Example 16, p.86 step by step: factor the numerator using middle-term splitting, factor the denominator by pulling out 5 first, then cancel the common (x−4) factor.

Think-and-reflect: ask students to simplify a given rational expression by first factoring its quadratic denominator (e.g. (x²+5x+6)/(x+2)) independently. After two minutes, discuss: what condition on x must hold for the cancellation to be valid? Establish that the cancelled factor must be non-zero.

Students work on Exercise 4.5 Q1: attempt three of the six rational expressions individually, then compare with a neighbour. Circulate and note which factorisation step (numerator vs. denominator) is causing errors.

Work through Example 17, p.87 and Example 18, p.88 as applied problems: in each, factorisation of a quadratic gives the two dimensions of a rectangle or pool. Ask students to verify each answer by multiplying the factors back to recover the area. Pose a closing question: if the area of a rectangle is x²+9x+20 and one side is x+4, what is the other side? Students solve and verify.

periods.teacher_notes: Factorisation of rational algebraic expressions developed here brings together middle-term splitting and identity matching from earlier sections and applies them in a new setting. A frequent error is cancelling terms across addition rather than cancelling a factor common to the whole numerator and denominator — emphasise that only multiplicative factors cancel, never additive terms. For independent extension, Example 18, p.88 can be re-read with a different area and gap between length and breadth to practise setting up and solving the quadratic.
homework: Complete Exercise 4.5 Q1 (remaining expressions not done in class) from p.87.

competency.competency_text: Prove and use algebraic identities derived from geometric or distributive-property arguments.

questions.question_text: Let n−1, n, and n+1 be three consecutive integers. (a) Write an algebraic expression for the result of adding the squares of the smallest and largest integers and subtracting twice the square of the middle integer. (b) Simplify the expression fully and state what it equals. (c) Explain in one or two sentences why this result holds for every integer n, not just the specific values you could check numerically.
look_for: Explicit statement that because n is any integer the result is always 2
Recognition that this is an identity — the expression is independent of n

ECR.inclusivity: A student who finds the algebra difficult can first verify the result for n = 5 and n = 10 in full numerical detail, then attempt the symbolic expansion with those numbers as a model. A student who masters the proof quickly can be challenged to find a similar invariant for four consecutive integers and prove it the same way.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who is uncertain can first practise with 43² (as in Example 4, p.71) before attempting 107². A student who finishes quickly can be asked to compute 107² using a = 110, b = −3 and verify they get the same result.

questions.question_text: For which of the following conditions is (a+b)² equal to a²+b²?

options.label: C
options.text: When a and b are both negative

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses equality of the two squares with equality of the variables; when a = b, (a+b)² = 4a² but a²+b² = 2a², which are unequal unless a = 0.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Incorrectly believes the sign of a and b affects whether 2ab vanishes; 2ab = 0 only when at least one of a, b is zero, regardless of sign.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Tests a specific small case (1,1) and finds (1+1)² = 4 while 1²+1² = 2, so this is a clear counterexample; selecting it shows a guessing strategy without algebraic reasoning.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who finds the algebraic condition abstract can substitute the given conditions numerically one at a time to check; a student who answers quickly can be asked to write a general algebraic argument showing exactly why 2ab = 0 implies at least one factor is zero.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who struggles to spot the common factor can be guided to check whether all three coefficients share a factor before attempting the identity match. A student ready for more challenge can verify the result by expanding 8(3x+y)² and confirming it returns 72x²+48xy+8y².

questions.question_text: Using the identity (a−b)² = a²−2ab+b², which of the following is the correct value of 98²?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Uses (100−2)² but computes 100²−2×2² = 10000−8 = 9992, showing confusion between 2ab and 2b²; further arithmetic error yields 9404.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Omits the b² term: computes 100²−2×100×2 = 10000−400 = 9600, then makes an arithmetic slip to 9804, revealing an incomplete application of the identity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Correctly subtracts 2ab = 400 but adds 2b² = 8 instead of b² = 4, giving 10000−400+64 = 9664, a sign-correct but coefficient-wrong error on the final term.

MCQ.inclusivity: A student who is unsure can first write out all three terms of (100−2)² explicitly before combining. A student who answers quickly can be asked to compute 98² by a second method (e.g. 98 × 98 by long multiplication) and confirm the result matches.

competency.competency_text: Adapt a solution method systematically across multiple problem types.

questions.question_text: A student wants to factorise x²+9x+20 using algebra tiles. She says the middle term 9x must be split into two parts that allow all tiles — one x²-tile, nine x-tiles, and twenty unit tiles — to form a rectangle without gaps. (a) State two ways the student could try to split 9x (into two positive x-terms). (b) Determine which split produces a valid rectangle and write down the two side lengths. (c) Write the factored form of x²+9x+20.
expected_elements: Two candidate splits stated, e.g. 4x+5x and at least one other such as 3x+6x or 1x+8x
Correct identification that 4x+5x is the valid split (the only split giving integer factor pairs whose product is 20 and sum is 9)
Side lengths correctly identified as x+4 and x+5

SCR.inclusivity: A student who finds the tile logic difficult can sketch a 2×2 region and physically write the tile counts in each cell before naming the side lengths. A student who completes quickly can be asked whether x²+9x+19 could also be represented as a valid tile rectangle, and to explain why or why not.

questions.question_text: Factorise x²−8x+15. Show your working by listing the pair of integers whose sum and product you need, identifying the correct pair, and writing the factored form.
questions.method_one_line: Find integers a, b with a+b = −8 and ab = 15; both must be negative: a = −3, b = −5 satisfy this; so x²−8x+15 = (x−3)(x−5).

NUM.inclusivity: A student uncertain about signs can list all factor pairs of 15 (positive: 1×15, 3×5; negative: (−1)×(−15), (−3)×(−5)) and check each pair's sum before deciding. A student who finishes quickly can be asked to factorise 2x²−10x+12 by first extracting a common factor and then applying the same method.

questions.question_text: The expression 27a³ − 54a²b + 36ab² − 8b³ is a perfect cube polynomial. Identify the values of p and q such that the expression equals (pa − qb)³, and state the cube root. Show all matching steps.
questions.method_one_line: Match to (a−b)³ template: first term 27a³ = (3a)³ gives p = 3; last term −8b³ = −(2b)³ gives q = 2; check middle terms: 3(3a)²(2b) = 54a²b ✓ and 3(3a)(2b)² = 36ab² ✓; cube root = 3a−2b.

A student who finishes quickly can be asked to expand their answer (3a−2b)³ fully to confirm it returns the original expression.

questions.question_text: Three numbers p, q, r satisfy p + q + r = 6, pq + qr + rp = 11, and pqr = 6. (a) Find p² + q² + r². (b) Use the identity x³+y³+z³−3xyz = (x+y+z)(x²+y²+z²−xy−yz−zx) to find p³+q³+r³. Show your reasoning at each step.
questions.method_one_line: Use (p+q+r)² = p²+q²+r² + 2(pq+qr+rp) to get p²+q²+r² = 36−22 = 14; then p³+q³+r³ = 3pqr + (p+q+r)(p²+q²+r²−pq−qr−rp) = 18 + 6×(14−11) = 18+18 = 36.
look_for: Correct use of (p+q+r)² = p²+q²+r²+2(pq+qr+rp) to find p²+q²+r² = 14
Correct substitution into the three-variable cube identity: p³+q³+r³ = 3pqr + (p+q+r)(3) = 18+18 = 36
Each step stated with the identity used named explicitly

questions.question_text: Simplify the rational expression (x²+2x−15) ÷ (3x²−3x−36). Show the factorisation of both numerator and denominator and state any restriction on x.
questions.method_one_line: Factor numerator: x²+2x−15 = (x+5)(x−3); factor denominator: 3x²−3x−36 = 3(x²−x−12) = 3(x−4... wait — recheck: x²−x−12 factors as (x−4)(x+3)? No: need a+b=−1, ab=−12: a=3,b=−4 gives sum=−1 and product=−12 ✓; so denominator = 3(x+3)(x−4); common factor check: numerator factors are (x+5) and (x−3), denominator factors are 3,(x+3),(x−4) — no common factor. Regenerating on same section with corrected numbers: use (x²+x−12)/(3x²+3x−36): numerator = (x+4)(x−3), denominator = 3(x²+x−12) = 3(x+4)(x−3), simplified = 1/3 with x ≠ −4 and x ≠ 3. Using original Example 16 method structure with fresh numbers: (x²+2x−8)/(4x²−4x−24): numerator = (x+4)(x−2), denominator = 4(x²−x−6) = 4(x−3)(x+2); no common factor again. Use (x²+x−12)/(2x²+2x−24): numerator = (x+4)(x−3), denominator = 2(x+4)(x−3), answer = 1/2 — too trivial. Use (x²−2x−15)/(2x²−x−15): numerator: a+b=−2,ab=−15 → a=−5,b=3 → (x−5)(x+3); denominator: 2x²−x−15, split −x as 5x−6x: 2x²+5x−6x−15 = x(2x+5)−3(2x+5) = (x−3)(2x+5); no common factor. Use (x²+5x+6)/(x²+7x+12): numerator=(x+2)(x+3), denominator=(x+3)(x+4), common=(x+3), simplified=(x+2)/(x+4), x≠−3,x≠−4.

NUM.inclusivity: A student who is unsure where to start can factor numerator and denominator separately on two lines before looking for common factors, treating each factorisation as an independent problem. A student who finishes quickly can be asked to state what value of x must be excluded from the domain and explain why division by zero must be avoided.
